newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania and Ukraine to sign historical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Romania and Ukraine to sign historical treaty.

text.p: Romania and Ukraine will on Monday sign a treaty setting aside historical differences which Bucharest hopes will bolster its chances of being chosen for fast-track NATO membership.

The treaty caps three years of attempts by the two neighbours to sign a post-communist accord and put behind them sensitive issues left over from an agreement signed nearly 60 years ago between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union under which Romania lost territories to Moscow.

The accord, to be signed by Romanian President Emil Constantinescu and his Ukrainian counterpart Leonid Kuchma, proclaims the present borders as "inviolable" and includes the remaining differences in a separate agreement.
The signing ceremony will take place in the Black Sea resort of Neptun, 250 km (160 miles) east of Bucharest.
Talks on the accord had been hampered by demands by Bucharest for Kiev to denounce the 1939 Ribbentrop-Molotov pact, which carved up Eastern Europe between Nazi Germany and Moscow.
Under the pact Moscow annexed the Romanian lands of Bukovina, southern Bessarabia and Serpent Island, now all part of Ukraine, as well as some half a million Romanians.
Kiev constantly rejected Bucharest's demands, saying they amounted to an overt territorial claim by Romania.
Differences related to delineating borders in the Black Sea, which both sides believe is rich in natural gas and crude oil, will be resolved separately by 1999, the treaty says.

The last few weeks have seen the two governments move towards a compromise, especially after Western democracies made clear that Romania's chances of getting into NATO would be improved by the absence of border conflicts and domestic ethnic disputes.
In a last-minute scramble to get early NATO admission, Bucharest in April said it was prepared to make "historic sacrifices" in its dealings with Ukraine and sign the treaty.

The signing ceremony on Monday had been timed with an eye to the NATO summit in Madrid in July, when the Alliance is expected to announce new members. Bucharest hopes its candidacy will be considered alongside the expected trio of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Romania's case for entry is backed by France, Spain, Italy and Greece. Key NATO members Germany and the United States have so far offered Romania understanding but no explicit support.
The treaty to be signed on Monday is expected to stir heated debates in parliament when presented for ratification.
Last month, Vadim Tudor, leader of the nationalist Greater Romania Party, called the treaty "an act of national treason" and urged Romanians to reject the accord through a referendum.
On Sunday many Bucharest residents said they were unhappy over the signing of the treaty with Ukraine.
"This means saying goodbye to Bucovina and Bessarabia for ever," Gabriel Nitu, 25, told Reuters.
Pensioner Gheorghe Constantinescu, 70, said the authorities "seemed to act counter to Romania's interest".
"I am totally against the treaty. It should say at least that those territories will return one day to Romania," he said.
Last year Romania won praise for signing a similar treaty with Hungary to end old rifts over borders and minorities.
